en: Daily Life for Entering the Assembly (*Wuliangshou Chanshi Riyong Xiaoqinggui*):

To transcend the mundane and leave secular life, one dons the shaven head and the square-cut robes; generally speaking, having passed through various monastic communities, it is essential to have a thorough understanding of their regulations and protocols.

Their conduct was unfamiliar with the laws and regulations, and their movements and pauses did not accord with the Vinaya. Although they were virtuous friends and good companions, how could they have been willing to apply the deep probe and the painful needle?
Having followed old habits until they became a malady, reform was indeed difficult; this caused the monastic assembly to fall into desolation and led people’s minds to grow indolent.
Frequently observing these common faults before one's eyes, I then gathered [the teachings] at Baizhang to establish a ready-made model.
From beginning to end, from morning until evening, one must strive to avoid failure at every turn; one must practice each and every instruction with precision.
Only then may one dare to speak of investigating the self and clarifying the mind, or of understanding life and penetrating death. The worldly dharma is itself the supramundane dharma.

This is something for those who have already set out on their journey to cherish, and for those who have not yet set out, it is a means to ensure they do not fail the very purpose of their monastic life. It is also, moreover, a restraint.
To repay the kindness and virtue of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, I have respectfully set forth the following.
The Method for Entering the Assembly: When sleeping, do not be ahead of others; when rising, do not lag behind others. One must rise quietly before the five-o'clock bell has sounded.
Lift the body first, placing the pillow under one's feet; do not fold it yet, for fear that its sound might startle others.
Neighboring the single mat, shake up your spirit and sit upright, wrapped in your robe. Do not fan the air to cause others to become distracted.
When you feel drowsy, push the robe beneath your feet, turn around, and step off the bed with a hand-towel.
Drape the towel over your left hand and recite this verse:
From the dawn of the morning until dusk, all sentient beings pass by one another.
If you should lose your physical form beneath your feet, I pray that you may immediately be reborn in the Pure Land.
Gently lift the curtain and exit through the rear gate. You must not slip off your sandals, nor cough or make any noise. As the ancients said: "Lift the curtain..."
One must hang down the trailing hand (when leaving the hall, one must strictly avoid wearing sandals). When washing the face with the basin, use light hands; the water should not be excessive.
When using tooth-cleansing powder, dip the right hand once to rub the left side of the mouth, and dip the left hand once to rub the right side.

One must not dip both hands again, for fear of passing on dental disease or bad breath to others. When rinsing the mouth and spitting out the water, one must lower the head and guide it with the hand.

[The text] continues below: One must not straighten the waist while spitting water so as to splash it into a neighbor’s bucket. One must not wash one’s head. There are four things that are disadvantageous to both oneself and others:

first, staining the bucket; second, staining the hand-towel—these two are disadvantageous to others; third, causing the hair to become matted; fourth, damaging the eyes—these two are disadvantageous to oneself.
One must not make sounds within the nostrils, nor should one vomit with a loud voice. As the ancients said: Five...
Washing the face is originally intended for the purpose of practice. After spitting into the basin, one must not make a clamor that disturbs the assembly.

Having wiped the face, one returns to the hall. If staying in the upper section, enter with the left foot first; if staying in the lower section, enter with the right foot first. Returning to one’s bedding position, fold the sitting mat (shanjian) in half before settling into the seated posture.
If changing into the *zhidie* robe, one must first drape the new one over the body; it must not [be worn in such a way as to expose the old one].
The moon is visible. One must not fan the air. When burning incense and prostrating, it is appropriate to do so before the bell has sounded.
Don the *kāṣāya* robe, first join the palms at the crown of the head and recite this verse:
Excellent is this robe of liberation, the signless field of merit. I now receive it upon my head;
may I always wear the folded *kāṣāya* throughout all lifetimes.
First fold it at the place where the hands rest, then unfasten the rings. One must not hold the *kāṣāya* in the mouth. One must not...
One should tuck the *kāṣāya* under the chin. Having finished folding it, one should also perform a formal greeting (*praṇāma*) before departing.

When performing prostrations in the hall or the main shrine, one must not occupy the center, thereby obstructing the arrival of the Abbot. One must not chant the Buddha’s name aloud. One must not pass by the side of a person walking; one must walk behind in an empty space.
At the striking of the bell for the fifth watch, the Abbot and the Head Seat shall sit in the hall; [others] must not [enter].
Enter and exit through the front gate. When entering the small meditation hall, fold the bedding and adjust the pillows. As for the method of folding the bedding:
first find the two corners and arrange them with your hands, extending them toward the front. First fold one half, then fold the front half.
Do not occupy the space of a neighboring bed by stretching it out horizontally. Do not shake it so as to make a noise. Do not use the bedding to fan yourself. Or...

Return to the communal quarters to consume medicinal decoctions or go to the tea hall. Following the sequence of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), return to your bowl position, turning with the upper shoulder in the proper direction (the upper shoulder refers to the left shoulder).
One must not enter with one's back toward the assembly. If entering through the front gate, one should enter from the southern side;

one must not walk along the northern side or through the center, as this would show disrespect for the Abbot. When the wooden fish gong sounds, one must not enter the hall, or else have an attendant do so.

Take the bowl and sit outside the hall, or return to the communal quarters. Upon entering the hall, return to your place for the bowls, bow low to pay respects to the seniors, middling seats, and juniors.
If you have already sat down when the seniors, middling seats, or juniors arrive, you must join your palms. As the ancients said:

"If one does not show respect to the seniors, middling seats, and juniors, there is no difference between this and a gathering of Brahmins. Upon hearing the long gong strike, lower the bowl, straighten your body, and stand up properly.

Once you have steadied yourself, turn around. You must also place your hands together at shoulder height to take the bowl. Support the bowl with one hand while the other hand releases the hook; lift it with your left hand.
Turn your body so that you face straight ahead, then squat down to set the bowl down, taking care not to strike others with your waist or back.

When the bell rings in front of the hall, descend from the platform and perform a formal greeting (*wenshen*). However, when welcoming the Abbot, there is no need to swing your arms to the left and right.
Dra. When descending from the bed, one must step forward to perform a greeting; do not allow the *kāṣāya* to drape over the cords of the bed, and remain humble and quiet.

When ascending the bed, do not throw the body down abruptly. Take the alms bowl and place it before you, then sit down. Upon hearing the sound of the wooden mallet, join the palms and recite the verse with mindfulness:
[Verse follows]
The Buddha was born in Kapilavastu, attained enlightenment in Magadha, preached the Dharma in Vārāṇasī, and entered parinirvāṇa in Kuśinagara.
Regarding the method of unfolding the alms bowl: first, join the palms and contemplate the verse.
The Tathāgata is the vessel of measure; now that I have obtained this opportunity for expansion, I pray that together with the entire assembly, the three spheres may be empty and quiescent.
Then, one should untie the head-wrap, spread the pure cloth to cover the knees, and fold the wrap so that its triangular end points downward, ensuring it does not [obstruct].
When exiting the hall, first spread out the bowl-cloth. With the left hand turned upward, take the bowl and place it upon the cloth.
Use the index fingers of both hands to pick up the bowl-rim and unfold it starting from the smallest end in sequence; do not let it clatter or make noise.

Furthermore, protect the fourth and fifth fingers (the ring and little fingers) as "defiled fingers" and do not use them to handle the bowl. Fold and crease it small, along with the bag for the spoon and chopsticks, and place it nearby.
Place the bowl horizontally. When entering [the dining hall], the spoon comes first; when leaving, the chopsticks come first. The part of the handle held by the hand is the "pure end" (*śuci-mukha*).

Hang the bowl-brush over the shoulder with its tip pointing upward, resting it within the seam of the second bowl-rim, protruding about half an inch. One must not use the spoon or chopsticks to hold raw rice.
When taking rice for the morning meal, do not exceed seven grains; too little is stinginess in eating. When the *karmadāna* chants the Buddha’s name, one should join the palms.
The fingers must not be uneven; they should be held at the chest, at the proper height. One must not rest the hands against the edge of the mouth. As the ancients said:
"Uneven palms not held at the chest, ten fingers interlaced and thrust into the nose, dragging sandals and lifting the curtain—[these are all improper]."
[The text] is detailed. Making a belching sound and releasing gas to display one's heroism; holding the bowl with both hands to receive food, one recites the verse:
"When receiving food, may all sentient beings take the joy of dhyāna as their nourishment, filled with the delight of the Dharma.
Whether the portion is more or less, one immediately uses the right hand to stop it. Upon hearing the signal for the universal distribution of food, one looks at the upper and lower shoulders.

Face the direction of the food. When receiving the food, do not face it directly; instead, move your hands to both sides. Once you have finished receiving it, perform the contemplation of the five reflections, saying:
1. Reflect on the labor involved and measure the distance from where it was brought. 2. Consider your own virtue and conduct to determine whether you are worthy of this offering.
Third, guarding the mind and remaining free from the faults of greed and so forth is the primary purpose; fourth, it is like excellent medicine for healing a withered body;
fifth, it is for accomplishing the work of the Path that one should accept this food.
As the birth verse says:
"You hosts of spirits and deities, I now offer this sustenance to you. This is the method for all spirits and deities throughout the ten directions to partake of food together:
bring the food to the mouth; do not bring the mouth to the food. [The rules for] taking up the bowl and setting it down, as well as..."
When using the spoon and chopsticks, one must not make noise. One must not cough. One must not wipe away mucus from the nose.
If one sneezes, one should cover the nose with the sleeve of one's robe. One must not scratch one's head, for fear that dandruff might fall into the neighboring bowl.
One must not pick at the teeth with the hand. One must not make noise while chewing food or sipping soup. One must not scoop rice from the center of the bowl. One must not form large mouthfuls.
When eating, one must not open the mouth to wait for food; one must not drop grains of rice; one must not eat by scattering rice with the hand.
If there are vegetable scraps, place them behind the bowl in a secluded spot. One must not fan one's neighbor with the breath;
if one is personally sensitive to the wind, inform the *karmadāna* and sit outside the hall. One must not rest the hands upon the knees. Receive food according to one’s capacity.
One must not ask for a reduction in the portion. One must not place wet food in the head bowl.
One must not use the soup broth in the head bowl to rinse rice. One must not pick at the vegetables. When eating rice mixed with other foods from the head bowl, one must look ahead and behind;
one must not eat too slowly. Before asking for more, one must not scrub the bowl. One must not make a sound by sucking on the bowl-brush. [This applies] when food has not yet arrived.
One must not give rise to afflictions. An ancient saying goes: "In his daze, he looks inward and gives way to grief and anger;
thinking of food, he swallows saliva and coughs repeatedly; he sips rice porridge and slurps soup with his mouth full; opening the mat and spreading out the bowl, his noise reaches all the neighbors.
When washing the bowl, one uses the head-bowl to hold water and washes the ladle in sequence. One must not wash the spoons, chopsticks, or the ladle inside the head-bowl. Furthermore—
Bend the fourth and fifth fingers. One must not make noise while rinsing or sipping water. One must not spit water into the bowl. One must not fill the bowl with hot water first.
When washing the bowl, one must not discard the water before it has been folded away. One must not gather the knee-cloth (jī-mo) beforehand.
One must not use the knee-cloth to wipe sweat. One must not pour leftover water onto the ground. One should recite the verse on discarding water while performing this act.
This water from my bowl-washing Is like the taste of celestial nectar (*amṛta*).
I bestow it upon you, the host of *pretas*, Causing all of you to be fully satiated. Oṃ mahoraga-se svāhā.
[Having finished,] hold the bowl with both hands, interlocking the index fingers and inserting them one after the other. Then, with palms joined, visualize [the deities] partaking of the food.
The concluding verse says:
When the meal is finished, physical strength and vitality are restored; His majestic power shakes the ten directions, he is a hero of the three periods of time.
Turning cause into effect without a thought, All sentient beings attain supernatural powers.
When the board in front of the quarters rings, one returns to the quarters to pay respects. Not returning is considered a slight against the assembly.

Upon entering the door and taking one’s place, follow the same procedure as in the Sangha Hall. Once standing in position and waiting for the abbot of the quarters (liao-zhu) to finish burning incense, pay respects to those above and below.
If there is tea, take your seat; do not let your robes hang down, do not huddle together talking or laughing, do not beckon others with one hand, and do not [cover your head].

Regarding the storage of tea leaves: the ancients said, "When sitting in formal meditation upon the platform, one must not let the robes hang loose. What kind of principle is it to beckon others with only one hand?
To privately store tea leaves is a cause for derision by onlookers. During the intervals between sessions, practitioners at neighboring tables must strictly avoid whispering into each other's ears.
After tea, when reading scriptures, one must not spread them out longwise—this refers to having both faces visible—and must not hold the scripture in one's hands.
While walking within the quarters, one must not let the sash hang down, nor make noise, nor lean against the headboard of the bench while reading scriptures.
As the ancients said: "To chant aloud is to disturb the crowd; to lean against the backboard is to show contempt for the assembly.

One should leave the quarters in advance and not wait until the sitting board is struck. If the robes become disarranged, according to ancient custom, one should cover them with the five-strip robe using a clean cloth.
With the left hand, untie the cord and fasten it to the top of the bamboo pole. Remove the hanging robe and adjust it so it is neat;
then secure it with a hand-towel. Furthermore, suspend the hand-towel about a chi below [the robe] to serve as a marker. One must not speak or laugh, nor may one urge others from outside.

Carrying water in the right hand, one enters the latrine and changes shoes so that they are not mismatched. Place the cleansing bucket in front; snap the fingers three times to alert the "feces-eating spirits.
One must squat with the body perfectly upright, never straining the breath to make noise, nor spitting phlegm or saliva.

One must not converse with others across the partition. As the ancients said: "When the door is closed, one should merely snap the fingers lightly; when people are crowded together, how can one bear to speak?"
Make no noise while entering. Use a tally-stick (*śalākā*) to divide the area for touching and cleaning.
When exiting, you must use water; avoid splashing it hither and thither. Do not pour water onto both sides. Wash with the left hand, protecting the thumb, second finger, and third finger.
Do not use too many tally-sticks. As the ancients said: "When using bath-water, use tally-sticks sparingly; do not pick up those already used. Once finished, rinse them with water."
Place it in an empty space at the side; as it will likely obstruct many people, it is not suitable for long-term placement.

Return the cleaning bucket to its original location. With dry hands, put on the inner garment and enter the trousers. In ancient practice, one opens the door with dry hands and exits carrying the bucket in the right hand.
One must not touch the door leaf or the door frame with wet hands. With the right hand, first scoop out the ash, and afterwards scoop out the earth. One must not...
One should not grasp ash or soil with wet hands, nor should one rinse one's hands by spitting into the mud.

Thereafter, wash with soap-nuts (sòjiǎo) up to the elbow, reciting the *Praveśa-mantra* for entering the latrine with each movement. Use water to rinse the mouth according to the ritual rules; even for minor urination, one must cleanse oneself thoroughly.
Then, chew a willow branch (*yángzhī*) and return to the hall to sit in meditation. One must not return to the quarters before the fire-board has sounded.
One must not wash clothes before the midday meal. One must not open chests or cabinets before the morning gruel, before the midday meal, or after the evening session.
If there is an urgent matter, inform the administrative officers; within the quarters, inform the head of the quarters; within the hall, inform the attendant of the Sacred Monk.
After the meal, one must not gather in groups to converse within the Sangha Hall, nor must one read sutras or books within the Sangha Hall.
One must not walk back and forth through the central aisle. One must not pass straight through the hall. One must not place coins upon a mat.
One must not sit with legs dangling over the edge of the bed. A space of one chi (approx. 30 cm) in front of the bed constitutes the "three pure areas":
first, for unfolding the alms bowl; second, for placing the *kāṣāya*; third, for the direction in which the head points. One must not walk upon the bed. One must not kneel on the bed to open a box.

Regarding the cabinet: one must not step onto the edge of the bed to descend to the floor. For those traveling the mountains with five-striped straw sandals (*sōri*), they must not perform walking meditation (*kankyō*) in the Buddha Hall or the Dharma Hall.
As the ancients said: "One may wear a robe tied at the side while ascending the hall, and straw sandals while traveling the mountains, but do not tread upon the Dharma Hall.

One should yield to seniors (*kishuku*). One must not go barefoot when wearing monastic shoes. One must not walk hand-in-hand with others discussing worldly matters of right and wrong. The ancients...
He said: "Having bid farewell to my parents and abandoned my original teacher, what do you intend to do by seeking out spiritual friends?
You have never spoken of the matters of the Zen school; that you have reached old age without success—whose fault is this? You must not lean against the palace pillars, nor must you run about wildly.
As the ancients said: 'Walk with measured steps and practice the majestic deportment of Aśvajit; speak in a low voice and learn [the conduct of Śāriputra].'"
The Precepts of Upāli: One must not wander idly within the Buddha Hall. As the ancients said: "If there is no business, do not ascend the jeweled hall;
do not casually enter the midst of the pagoda. If one does not sweep the floor or add scented water, even the merit of the Ganges sands will eventually be exhausted.
After the midday meal, when washing clothes, one must not expose the torso. One must not pour hot water from the pitcher directly onto the clothes on a bamboo pole.
When the ironing board has been used, place it in its designated spot. When the foot-washing board sounds, do not scramble for the foot-tub;

if you have sores or scabies, wash them immediately afterward in a secluded area to avoid disturbing the minds of others. Do not wait for the striking of the board for the sitting hall. Return to the hall in order to practice seated meditation.
After the formal session ends, fold the bedding halfway on one’s mat and leave it in front of the quarters. As soon as the board sounds, [proceed to the hall].

At that time, turn your body toward the outside; you must act with due timing. When the small wooden board (small-pan) sounds for the assembly, you must not enter the hall, nor may you stand outside the hall.
When the Abbot and the Head Seat exit the hall, they open their mats and descend from their seats to perform a formal greeting (*wensun*).

Upon returning to the quarters, the medicinal food (*yaoshi*) is each placed upon one’s assigned seat. One must not rise first to serve the food, nor may one call out loudly to demand porridge, rice, salt, or vinegar.
Those of this class, having finished their meal, shall leave the quarters. They must not go out through the three gates, nor enter small quarters.

They must not leave their robes unfastened while returning to the Sangha hall or walking along the corridors. They must not wait for the striking of the board to leave the quarters. When the evening bell tolls, they shall immediately join their palms and recite the verse as follows:
Hearing the sound of the bell, afflictions are lightened; wisdom grows, and Bodhi arises.
Departing from hell, emerging from the fiery pit, may we vow to attain Buddhahood and deliver all sentient beings.
One must first return to one's room and sit in meditation. One must not scratch one's head on the bed, nor fiddle with prayer beads on the bed.

One must not make noise. One must not converse with those on the beds of neighboring quarters. If one’s neighbors are strangers, one should win them over with kind words and must not harbor feelings of resentment or dislike.
Until the wooden fish (dingzhong) has been struck, one must not enter or exit through the front gate.

As for the head seat (shouzuo), if the sound of the fire-bell (huoling) does not reach his pillow, he is not permitted to open the incense burner. For prostrations, one must wait until it is even deeper in the night. The assembly...
One must not go to sleep before others have slept; one must rise before the assembly has risen. When rising from or sitting on one's seat, one must not disturb those in neighboring cells.

When sleeping, one must lie on the right side; one must not lie on the back. To lie on the back is the sleep of a corpse; to lie face down is the sleep of a lecher, both of which result in many evil dreams.
One should wrap the *kashāya* (monastic robe) in a cloth and place it at the head of the pillow. Nowadays, people often place it at their feet, which is contrary to principle.
When it is time for the bath, take the bathing requisites in your right hand and enter within the threshold of the lower section to perform a greeting. Return to your empty space;
after you have finished bowing to those on your left and right, first hang your five-strip towel on the bamboo rack.
Unfold your bath robe, take out the bathing requisites, and set them aside. Remove your upper garment, but do not discard your *zhiduo* (straight robe) immediately; first take off the lower garment.
Regarding the robes: wrap the foot-towel around the body and fasten the bathing skirt. Roll up the undergarments and trousers and place them inside the outer robe.
Next, remove the *zhiduo* (upper robe) and the five-strip robe (*wutiao*) and set them aside together. Tie the hand-towel to the bamboo pole; if there is no hand-towel, use a cord to tie it.
The ancients said: When entering the hall at the third signal of the bath drum, one must distinguish between the upper and lower garments for the sake of purity and cleanliness.
Having removed the remaining clothes, they should be folded together and placed aside. One must not enter the bath barefoot; one must wear wooden clogs.
One should draw water from an empty space in the lower section and must not occupy the seats of the elders or senior practitioners—meaning those in the upper section. One must not...
One must not splash hot water onto another person’s body. One must not place a bucket on the ground to soak one's feet.
One must not relieve oneself or wash in secluded areas within the bathhouse. One must not rest one's feet upon the bucket. One must not speak or laugh.

One must not scrub one's feet on the wooden trough. One must not bail out the water. One must not stand up and lift the bucket to pour water over oneself, for fear of splashing water onto those nearby.
Those who enter before or after you must provide mutual protection for one another. You must not use excessive amounts of bath water on your entire body. Your foot-towel must never leave your person.

If there is someone with a foot-towel who does not enter the tub—perhaps because they have a sore, or are washing a scar from moxibustion, or are applying ointment for scabies—they should enter the bath last.
One must not use the communal hand-towels placed at either side to wipe the head or face; these are the hand-towels designated for the bathhouse.

After putting on the robes, wash your hands and don the vestment (*kaṣāya*). Upon exiting the bath, bow to those on your left and right. First put on the upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*) and the *zhiduō* (straight-cut robe).
Once fully covered, put on the lower garment (*antarvāsaka*). Remove the bathing skirt and unfold the foot-towel inside it, fearing that the bathing cloth might get wet.
Carry the hand-towel in your left hand; you must not drape the damp foot-towel over your arm. Bow to those on your left and right as you exit.
Look at the names of the donors who have provided the bath; recite sutras and mantras as you wish and dedicate the merit.

In the cold months, when warming oneself by the fire, first sit upon the hearth, then turn your body to enter the furnace. After paying your respects, you may sit. Those who are devout must remove their shoes outside.
One must not fiddle with the incense spoons or fire tongs, nor poke at the fire, nor huddle together to talk, nor roast food or light lamps.
One must not heat objects such as shoes, socks, or clothing on the fire; this includes roasting one's feet or drying garments, all of which are prohibited.
One must not pull up the *zhidu* (straight robe) to expose the hem of the trousers underneath. Furthermore, one must not spit or blow sputum and grime into the brazier.
As previously compiled, these daily affairs and the protocols for the assembly are not intended to be heard by the experienced and mature; they are offered merely to guide beginners.

Whether ascending the hall, entering the room, holding a small sermon, chanting scriptures, reciting mantras, touring the quarters, untangling knots, attending to visitors, packing one’s belongings, donning the straw hat, conducting funeral rites, or presiding over the distribution of robes—all such subtle rules of conduct are already fully recorded in the *Chanyuan Qinggui* (Pure Rules of the Chan Monastery).
The venerable masters each have clear records of this; I shall not present them again in full detail, as it would merely result in redundant speech.

Recorded respectfully by the bhikṣu Zongshou at the quarters of the Chief Seat (Shouzuo) on Qian’guifeng, on the Buddha’s Birthday in the second year of the Jiading era, the Year of Jisi (1209). (End)
